column1: # Unification is the most fundamental thing core does after dispatch, and
# until this file existed no corpus row touched it. The reason was
# structural rather than an oversight: unify's clients — `is`, `case`,
# typed defs, record shapes — are all basic/lang-layer words, so a bare
# core registry called the unifier from nowhere, and core/spec's notation
# could name seven builtin type literals and no type CONSTRUCTOR at all.
# Two additions open it, and both are in the established idiom:
#   unifyq a b   the fixture word, over core's own UnifyR / unifiesValue.
#                The PREDICATE half only — did the two values unify — not
#                the unified value: Go's UnifyR returns a meet and core/ts
#                has a predicate, so asking for the value would pin a port
#   d( … )       a disjunct of the listed items
#   [: T … ]     a typed list — child constraint, then retained elements
#   {: T k: v … }  a typed map, likewise
# The type-constructor forms are what make this corpus reach the surface
# the two ports actually differ on. Without them every candidate agreed:
# 70 of 70 over scalars, lattice roots, plain lists and plain maps. That
# negative result is worth as much as the divergences — it says the value
# subset core/ts implements is FAITHFUL, and the gap is entirely in the
# constructors it has no arm for.
# --- the shared subset: scalars, roots, plain containers -------------------
# Every one of these agreed on first measurement.
run unifyq { a: 1 b: 2 } { b: 2 a: 1 }
run unifyq { a: { b: 1 } } { a: { b: 1 } }
run unifyq { a: { b: 1 } } { a: { b: 2 } }
# --- type constructors: what the two ports DO agree on ---------------------
# The rest of this surface is in divergent.tsv; these are the rows that hold.
run unifyq true d( Integer String )
run unifyq d( Integer String ) Any
# Closed by the payload gate in unifiesValue: a typed map is no longer
# handed to asMap(), so these answer cleanly instead of throwing.
